An app intent is a structure that implements the protocol, which defines the required behavior for all app intents.
You use this structure to provide the basic information about your app intent’s action, and to store the data and code you need to perform the action.
However, if you support app intents from one of the system-defined schemas, you can also use Xcode code completion to generate it for you.
To use Xcode code generation to create your initial type, type the domain you support followed by an underscore character and select an app intent from the list Xcode provides.

People use Siri AI to interact with content that’s visible onscreen, but that content is private to your app.
People use apps to view and interact with their content, but they can also interact with that content in other ways.
Someone might use Siri while driving to perform actions using your app, like sending a message or creating a note.
With the App Intents framework, your code remains the source of truth and you use the framework’s protocols and other types to make your content available to the system.
An app intent defines one of your app’s actions and the data you require to perform that action, and the system uses the app intents you create as the gateway to your app’s features.
Make sure each app intent performs a unique action within your app, and use its parameters to configure it for different types of data.

For example, instead of creating one app intent to play songs and a separate app intent to play albums, create a single app intent to play music and use a parameter to specify which song or album to play.
Whether you define a custom app intent or use one of the predefined schemas, the protocol defines the common behaviors for all app intents.
Use this protocol, or one of several as the starting point for your app intent type.
Each app intent you create needs to have the following minimum set of behaviors: It performs an action in its method.
It declares any required or optional parameters it needs to perform the action.

To differentiate entities from one another in the index, Spotlight uses the entity’s unique identifier, which the protocol requires you to provide.
When indexing your app’s content, use a named type and not the default index.
Use the default index only for prototyping and testing your code during development.
